utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the interpreters. I can hear you too. Thank you. The technical booth, the legal assistants, the Prosecution, the Defence, the court reporters, General Krstic. Good morning to you all. I also wish the public good morning. We already have a witness in the courtroom. I think it is Witness P. You're now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: WITNESS P

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Are you comfortable, Witness P?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please be at ease. I think it is Mr. Harmon who is going to put questions to you, so for the moment you will be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor. Excuse me. Yes, there is a minor matter that we have to attend to. Witness P, the registrar is going to show you a piece of paper with your name written on it. Look at it, please, and tell us, simply by saying yes or no, whether that is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is your name indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So, Mr. Harmon, you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours; good morning, counsel; good morning, Witness P. Mr. President, before I begin my examination of Witness P, I just want to inform Your Honours that after Witness P we have one additional witness to call for today, and at the end of the testimony of the second witness we would like to introduce some documents. The introduction of those documents will not take more than 15 minutes. So we can schedule the day accordingly. I bring that to Your Honours' attention and I will now commence my examination of Witness P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Allow me to say to you that all the witnesses are very special.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, could you tell us how old you are?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the creation of the UN safe area of Srebrenica, were you a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 16th of June, 1992, by orders of the army command, or rather the Territorial Defence. I was appointed to working on the collection of humanitarian aid in the local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So following your injury you were released from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time of the fall of the enclave in July of 1995, were you a member of the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention on the fall of the enclave in July of 1995, specifically on the 11th of July, 1995. At that point in time were you married and did you have children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was married and had four children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could you tell the Judges what happened on the 11th of July that caused you and your family to go in different directions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We simply received orders from the civilian structures that we had -- all of us had to go to the enclave of Srebrenica. Our assignment was that all of us should go towards Susnjari, especially the men, whereas the men [sic] and women went to UNPROFOR, to Potocari. We got to a hill called Lehovici, where we split up. So all the women and children went to the battalion compound in Potocari and the men towards Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why was there a distinction between where the women went and where the men went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply we didn't dare. We didn't dare go to Potocari. We couldn't trust them. So only the women and children dared go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "we couldn't trust them," who are you referring to as "them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs, because when they captured the enclave, they controlled the UN. They took their vehicles. They occupied the enclave. So we didn't dare go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Susnjari, how many men gathered -- men and boys gathered at that location, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The figure ranged between thirteen and fifteen thousand, according to the municipal authorities. The figure could not be established, but I think it was between thirteen and fifteen thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know the range of ages of those males who had gathered at Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 16 to 50 or 60 maybe. Though there were some women, or rather girls, who followed their boyfriends there, men. A smaller number of women, maybe some 200 or 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the number of men amongst that group who were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about one third had weapons in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I understand that the people in that group of approximately 15.000 people left the enclave in a column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The column was formed. The order was that we had to pass through Serb lines. So it was about 7.200 kilometers to free territory, to Tuzla, so we had to break through the lines. And the column was formed at the very entrance to the place Buljim, so this column was some ten kilometers long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in which direction did the column advance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It advanced towards Konjevic Polje. We passed Nova Kasaba and then on towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness P, I'm not going to ask you questions about your experiences in the woods -- perhaps the Judges would like to inquire about that, perhaps counsel will inquire about that -- but I want to fast-forward the experiences that you had to the 13th of July, when there was a decision taken by you and by others to surrender to the Bosnian Serb army. Can you tell the Judges, did you surrender, and can you tell the Judges why you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My group -- a relative of mine was seriously wounded, my cousin, and there was a small group left of some 30 men. The night between the 12th and the 13th we were cut off from the big column. We were in a stream. It was foggy. We didn't know where we were. In the morning there was heavy shelling. Shells were falling around us. There was an ultimatum. They were calling us out on the loudspeaker that we had to surrender, that we should carry the wounded, that we should be exchanged, according to the Geneva Conventions, that no one would be heard. There was a lot of hesitation amongst us whether we should try to pull out or to surrender to the Serb soldiers at Kravica. And after a time they said they would begin the countdown, and the order was to collect the wounded. A number of people were killing themselves, committing suicide. They didn't want to surrender. When we carried down the wounded to Kravica, a column was formed towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said a number of people committed suicide. Did you see people commit suicide, and do you know why they did commit suicide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did see it. I don't know. There were poisons that were being thrown, poisonous gases, and people lost control. They knew more or less what lay in store for them, that they would be killed or put into camps. And I saw two brothers. I don't know their names. First they embraced each other. They had an automatic rifle. There was a scream. They opened a burst of fire to one another. Then there was another group of people that threw a bomb into the group, and then four or five of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness P, I'm going to ask you to talk just a little bit slower, because the interpreters need to follow your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me now the group of people who threw the bomb they were from the group of Muslims or the group of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the people that threw the bomb that you just testified about, were they Muslims committing suicide or were they Serbs killing Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Muslims who were killing themselves. I heard that they may have been Serbs too. At that moment, I couldn't distinguish one from the other. They were all mixed together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the poisonous gases, they were thrown by the Muslims to commit suicide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the shells with poisonous gases. I could feel it myself, my eyes were stinging and one was very thirsty and one could feel it on one's own skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness P, how many people along with you went down to surrender on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that there may have been some 30 men in my group; I didn't count them. We had four or five wounded. And on the asphalt road, we came across a large group that had surrendered at Konjevic Polje, there were 300 or so people and they had some 20 wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to move away from the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've been asked by the interpreters if you can move a little bit away from the microphone. Now, Witness P, when you surrendered to the Bosnian Serb soldiers. Can you describe their appearance, how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms in dark blue, dark blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any people in dark green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see. At that moment, I didn't really distinguish. We were all frightened. I know that they all had camouflage uniforms. Whether they were lighter in colour or darker in colour, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do you know the difference between police camouflage uniforms and army camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't, but later I saw on television that there was a difference, but at that moment, I really can't remember whether there was any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Tell the Judges what happened after you surrendered; where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we carried down the group of wounded to Konjevic Polje, this group of mine, between 250 and 300 men. The order was to lay down the wounded at the cross roads at Konjevic Polje. One of the Serbs told us that they would take over the care of the wounded. They put us up in a hangar which used to be a kind of shopping area and some people started bringing water, but it wasn't enough. There were only two or three bucket fulls of water. We stayed there for some 20 minutes and then the order came to get on to trucks. I ran out and I saw three or four trucks. I don't remember exactly whether there were three or four. They were parked at the very crossroads at Konjevic Polje. The trucks were facing Milici and Nova Kasaba. The trucks were covered with canvas. I couldn't see, and I don't remember the licence plates nor whom they belonged to but I think they were civilian trucks. They had canvas covers, and I think they belonged to the Boksit company, I think. I'm not sure. And we had to climb on to the trucks and the truck I was in started towards Nova Kasaba. Then we passed a sports field that used to be used before the war, and the order was to get off the bus, the truck, I'm sorry. When we started getting off to our right-hand side, I saw a group of Serb soldiers who were waiting for us there. The order was that all the equipment that we had on us, except for money and gold, which they had taken from us at the very beginning in Kravica, that we had to throw those things on to a big pile. And there was a big pile of bags and backpacks and there were some poplar trees there, and we got off the truck in a line and entered this stadium. The stadium was full of men. According to my estimate, there were between 2.500 to 3.000 men and they were all sitting there in a -- within the compound. And my group that got off the trucks, we formed a new row there in the playground, sports field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me have Prosecutor's Exhibit 12/4 and place this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, I'm going to ask you if you can identify this location that's depicted in this image. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the stadium at Nova Kasaba. This is the goal [indicates]. And we stopped here somewhere next to the trees. This is the road to Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, and this is where I entered the stadium [indicates], the sports field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating for the record that the entry into the stadium was midway along the line of trees that boarders the road that goes from the top of the image to the bottom of the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this stadium, this football field, is the location where you said there were thousands of men on it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm finished with that image. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, was the football pitch -- how many men were on the pitch and how much of the area of the football field was covered by those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. You mean the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask it again. Did the Bosnian Muslim men cover the entire football pitch, half of the pitch, a quarter of the pitch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the whole pitch was covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you see Bosnian Serb soldiers in and around the Muslim men who were detained at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb soldiers, about 15 to 20 of them were waiting for us at the very entrance gates armed with rifles and they gave us orders. They swore at us and ordered us to enter the pitch. Within the pitch itself, around us who were sitting there, there were Serb soldiers with their guns pointed at us. They were swearing and giving us orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you estimate the number of soldiers that you saw around you and the other men at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact estimate because, after all, it was a long time ago, but there were 15 to 20 at the very entrance. As for the total, in any case, there were many in the field, at least 100 or so. But that may not be the correct figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also they had camouflage uniforms on. On one soldier, I couldn't notice any rank. He may have had insignia, but they all had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, continue with your -- describing your experiences at the football field, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So when my group entered and when we sat down, after some 15 or 20 minutes behind my back I saw an APC of olive-green colour arriving, and I saw several soldiers around the personnel carrier. And then a big man came out of the APC, some 30 to 40 metres away from me. And when he passed by me, he turned around and asked whether we recognised him. I knew him from the media and he introduced himself. He said that he was the commander of the Serb army, that he was General Ratko Mladic. He was a heavy man with a short cut, well-shaved with some receding hairlines in a short-sleeved shirt. And when he stood in front of us, I don't remember whether it was a podium or a couple of steps, I don't know. He started insulting and cursing us. "Where is your state? What are you dying for? Where is your Alija? Where is Haris Silajdzic? Where are your leading commanders? Naser Oric and Zulfo Tursunovic. You are laying down your lives and you've left your women and children for us to care for them." And there were other such insulting words and then the -- at the end he said, "Your authorities in Tuzla don't want you. So we will put you up. Our troops will give you water and food, and then we'll see whether we'll send you to Krajina, to Fikret Abdic or to the Bijeljina camp to the Batkovici camp in Bijeljina." Then orders came for us to get up, to get on to the trucks. I was towards the end of the field, and we headed towards the trucks. I also saw the trucks waiting on the road, three or four trucks, and I think there was a bus belonging to Boksit Trans from Milici. They were waiting on the road in front of the exit from the playing field. My group of men who -- the group that was moving with me, when we were going through the gates, someone said that we should pick up the bags. And Serb soldiers were guarding the gates and the bags. One of the group of Serb soldiers said to us, "You won't need that any longer." Probably they were thinking of what they were going to do. And so we got on to the trucks again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there for a moment, Witness P, and ask you two questions. Do you remember approximately what time of the day it was when you and others started to board the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about 1700 hours or 5.00 in the afternoon. Somewhere around 5.00, between 5.00 and 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the statement made by the Bosnian Serb soldier that you wouldn't need your bags anymore made at about that same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As we were leaving the football pitch and about to climb on to the trucks, I heard one of the Serb soldiers saying when one of our men wanted to pick up his bag. I heard him telling him, "You won't need that bag anymore."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My last question about this part of your experience: Did you receive any food and any water while you were at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. Far from it. I don't know whether anyone asked for any water, but none was distributed anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I interrupted you, Witness P, when you were recounting your story about getting on to the truck. Would you please carry on from that point in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So we climbed on to the truck. I don't know how many trucks there were that became full at that point. My truck started out right away. There was an order for the trucks to move. So we went in the direction of Konjevic Polje, that is along the same road we had used to come there, to get there. When we reached the junction with Konjevic Polje, the truck turned right again in the direction of Bratunac. And then we arrived in Kravica. I knew Kravica very well because I had passed through Kravica on a number of occasions before the war. And we stopped near a supermarket. My truck -- well in my truck, we happened to count ourselves, and there were 119 people on my truck. We were sitting on each other's laps on the floor, on the bed of the truck with our legs crossed. I was towards the rear part of the truck which was covered by canvas. Those were very large canvases, and at the back of the truck, you could see through because there was a half a metre opening at that point. So I told you I was sitting in the back of the truck. And as the truck was turning right, I saw that there were two trucks behind us. All of them were facing the direction of Bratunac. It was getting dark at that point, and people were getting nervous. The Serb soldiers who were guarding the trucks, who were standing guard around the trucks started mistreating people, hitting them with rifle butts through the canvas of the trucks. They would hit people who sat next to the side of the truck and they went on torturing them. Then they asked about people from specific villages from around the area of Srebrenica, the villages of Glogova, Osmac and other villages. I don't know why they asked for people from those villages. If anyone stood up, they would take him out. We spent the whole night on the trucks and we could hear screams, moaning, cries for help. Screams again. People shouting, "Please, don't beat me. Don't kill me. Don't butcher me." It was so terrible, it was so -- we couldn't take it anymore. I know that five people were taken off my truck during that night. I didn't see them being killed there on the spot, but they didn't come back to the truck. I don't know their names. And bursts of gunfire could be heard throughout the night, coming from around the trucks, and the screams of people, and this lasted all night long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, were there two other trucks parked --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Harmon, but I think there is a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 10.08 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume, Mr. Harmon. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, the technical problem has been resolved and we'll continue with your testimony. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have placed on the ELMO, to your right, a map, and I'd like you to take a look at that map. And if you could use the pointer, first of all, could you point to the location where you were detained at the football field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the football field, this was here, between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you were taken in a truck to a different location, where you spent the night, and you've just been describing your experiences at that location. Could you point to that location for the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we went back towards Konjevic Polje, and then towards Sandici and Kravica [indicates]. And this was all along the road towards Bratunac. And this is where we spent the night, on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the pointer is on the village of Kravica. Thank you, Witness P. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Witness P, focusing your attention on the night of the 13th and the early morning hours of the 14th, while you were in the truck, did you receive any water? Did you receive any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were in the truck, during the morning we got only one bucket of water. I don't know who it was who brought the water, but it was hardly a drop for all of us. You can image. It was only one jerrycan of water, and we were 119. We didn't get any food either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, do I understand your testimony correctly that in addition to your truck that was at that location in Kravica, there were two other trucks nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see behind my truck two additional trucks. Whether there were any other trucks, I don't know. I couldn't guarantee. I know that there were two more trucks, so in total there would have been three trucks, including mine. I don't know whether there were any trucks ahead of us. That I couldn't see because of the canvases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the type of uniform being worn by the Bosnian Serb soldiers who were in and around your truck on the night of the 13th and the early morning hours of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that they all had a camouflage uniform. To be perfectly honest, I couldn't tell the difference. I wasn't familiar with that. And then we were in great fear. We had been beaten and we didn't dare look outside. People were cursing at us all the time. They were mistreating us. And I know that there was one young man who did not cross over. A Serb soldier put a gun, the barrel of his gun, in his mouth. And the situation was terrible. It was so hot. It was stuffy. People didn't have any water, any food. And somebody tried and asked for water. It was total chaos. And at one point we could hear screams. It was complete madness. We could hear curses, and this soldier cursed his balija mother and he put a barrel of his gun into his mouth. I don't know this man. And he did not reach the free territory. But the soldier told me, "I will kill you and ten other people if I hear another word being uttered in the truck." And then everything went silent, and then perhaps after 20 minutes or half an hour, people started screaming again, asking for water, for help, and I could see people drinking their own urine, trying to moisten their lips with their own urine. So you can image how it was, and it was all in terrible heat under the canvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you estimate how hot it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outside temperature must have been around 28 or 30 degrees, so I don't know how hot it would have been under a canvas. I don't know what the temperature would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you remain at that location in Kravica before you were transported to a different location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Kravica, on the 14th of July, when it dawned, mistreatment started again, and we spent the whole day in the truck again. And sometime in the afternoon -- nobody had a watch. It had all been taken away from us on the first day when we surrendered. Nobody had any watch, therefore. But I know that it must have been in the afternoon, between 2.00 and 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point I heard somebody say that we were going to Batkovic, that the trucks were leaving for the Batkovic camp. And the trucks that had been facing Bratunac turned around and started back towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And after the trucks reached Konjevic Polje, in which direction did they travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So my truck continued right, in the direction of Zvornik, and I could see, driving right behind us, maybe some 10 meters away from us, started moving as well. This truck was escorted by two Serb soldiers with rifles, who -- one of them was sitting next to the driver and the other one was also in the cabin of the truck and he was holding his rifle out through the window. It was pointing out. And we had been told earlier on in Kravica that should anyone try to jump out of the truck, that they would kill ten people. So I know that my truck was moving in the direction of Zvornik. We reached Zvornik. I knew the place very well. But we passed through and continued after Zvornik, and this is where women and children started throwing rocks and stones on the buses. We continued then towards Karakaj, towards the aluminum factory in Karakaj. That area was no longer familiar to me, but we didn't travel for very long, and at one point the truck turned left. It was already evening. We didn't travel for very long, maybe only for about 15 minutes after Karakaj, after the factory. The truck therefore turned right, and we could see the trucks stopping, coming to a halt. I could see that there was a schoolyard in the area, like a small playground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, let me stop you there for a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could have 1/E/1 again placed on the ELMO, the small map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'd just like you to indicate on this small map the direction of travel that you took from Kravica up to the area past Zvornik. And I think the map will have to be opened up. And just use the pointer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kravica [indicates], Konjevic Polje [indicates], then we go down the river to the right of Konjevic Polje, we come to Zvornik, Karakaj, and somewhere there, to the left from Karakaj, we came to the school. Between the Dam and Karakaj, that is where the school was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for the record, I think it's fairly clear from his description the route he took between Konjevic Polje and the Drina River. He crossed the Drinjaca River. The rest I think is very clear. He progressed up along the Drina River, past Zvornik, to Karakaj, and left to an area near Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness P.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm finished with the exhibit, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how long did it take you to travel from Kravica to the school that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me see. When we travelled by public transport, it took about an hour, an hour and a half to reach Zvornik. So this was a little bit further, so about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you tell the Judges what happened to you and to the other men once you arrived at the playground at the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the playground of the school, I heard sporadic shooting. Then there was noise, cursing, yelling. And suddenly my truck stopped, and when it stopped I saw two other trucks in addition to mine, facing forward at the school playground. The order was that we jump off the trucks, one by one, and as we jumped off, the order was to put our hands up behind our heads and to chant aloud, "Long live the Serb Republic" and "Srebrenica is Serb," and maybe a few other words that I haven't remembered. And as we were jumping out of the trucks and running, Serb soldiers, in my estimate, some 20 or so, between the truck and the school, formed two lines. And as we ran between them, I said that we had to run and chant those words. And usually everyone got hit, some with a rifle butt on the back. Some were kicked, some were slapped. And then we ran towards the school. Towards the school there were some steps, five or six steps going down, so that the first level was lower than the yard itself. There was a double door, and we ran into the school, into a corridor. There was a short hall. And again there were soldiers there who were hitting us and beating us, and they directed us to the right, up some steps leading upstairs. There were several steps and then there's a kind of landing and then the steps turned left to the second floor. When I reached the second floor, as I was running I could see that there was an iron railing in the corridor, and the classrooms were lined one next to another. I know that I entered classroom number 3. 1, 2, 3. Whether there was another classroom further on, I'm not sure, but I think there was some other rooms further down. When we entered the classroom, I saw that it was a school, and on the left-hand side of this classroom there was a blackboard, and on the floor were some vinyl tiles, those that are glued on. There were no school desks. All the windows were closed. And it was stuffy, because we had travelled under the canvas in the trucks. And as soon as I entered I saw two men who had been badly beaten up and covered in blood. At first glance I thought they were dead. I knew one of them in person. He's Munib Admovic, who was very badly beaten. I could describe him. He had a cap and a jacket. I thought he was dead. So we all sat down in rows. We had to form those rows from the windows forward. The windows could not be opened. There were two soldiers standing at the doorway all the time, and they told us that we musn't open the windows, that we must sit there, that we would be given food and water. And so it went on until the classroom was full. As soon as it was filled up, other soldiers started barging in, demanding money. They gave us 15 or 20 minutes, otherwise 20 would be killed, if we didn't collect a certain sum of money. I don't know how much they said. They would close the door and go out, and say, "Not a word." The men were tired as a result of high temperatures. They didn't have any water, and they started yelling again, and again they would come through the door, take people out, and one could hear bursts of fire and shooting around the school. No one dared look through the window to see what was happening outside. Suddenly a young man tried to look out, and someone shot him, and he was wounded in that classroom. They said, "If anyone had money left in Srebrenica, that they had hidden, let him tell us and we would take a car and go to Srebrenica, and that man would be saved and transported to Tuzla." However, nobody said they had any money, because this was the third time they were searching us thoroughly and taking everything away. Suddenly, a relative, a neighbour of mine, asked for water. However, he was turned back. A second time when he went to look for water, he walked out the door and he never came back. We could hear fire all the time. Darkness was beginning to fall. I personally didn't feel well. I was having problems. I was feeling dizzy. I somehow got close to the window to get some air, and in my estimate, there were about 200 men in that classroom. And what happened, I don't really know myself. Suddenly when I came to a little, I could see that there were only a few men left in the classroom, 15 to 20, and I could see on those tiles blood and water, or rather urine, and then I saw Munib Admovic, who was trying to get up, and I asked him, "What has happened?" And he couldn't give me an answer. Shortly after that two came in from the outside, two soldiers, and gave orders, "The next four now." And I saw that I had to get up. I and Kadrija Becirevic, who was with me, and two other men, I don't know. We went out together. When we reached the corridor in front of that classroom, next to the iron railing, there were four to five Serb soldiers in uniforms as well, and they ordered us to take off everything, to strip. And I saw a whole pile of clothing and footwear and documents, ID cards, medical ID cards, driving licences and that sort of thing. I took off my shoes, my socks. I only had my vest on, and they let me keep that on. We had to turn out the pockets of our trousers, every little piece of paper, so make sure there was nothing left. What was the reason for this, I don't know. And so we had to stand against this iron railing and the order was to put our hands behind our backs which is what I did. And I saw next to those soldiers a ball of string or rather rope. And I saw him cutting pieces of that rope and tying my hands twice around. There may be pictures somewhere how they tied me up. And he was a big man. He was fair. I don't know him. He just asked me where I was from. When I told him where I came from, he slapped me, he cursed my balija mother, and he pushed me opposite classroom number two. Classroom number two was open, the door was open then, and there was no light on. When I fell, I fell on a friend of mine. He hasn't come either. They were all tied up in that classroom. I couldn't say much, I just asked him, "What is happening?" He couldn't give me an answer. I knew then that the end was approaching. Some 15 or 20 minutes later until all these men had come out and were tied up, I heard the order, somebody yelling, "Send me ten." And the man at the door said, "Get out, ten of you." And I was near the door, and as a group we ran out with our hands tied down the steps. And when I started down the steps, I saw in that corridor or I could feel under my bare feet that there was blood. And in the hallway at the bottom of the steps, three to four men lying dead in the hallway of the school. In front of the school there was a truck. It was already night-time, I don't know what time it was, but I think it was after midnight. And the truck was standing there, the back part facing the entrance to the school. The back side was down. And so with our hands tied, barefooted, naked to the waist had to climb into the truck which was covered with a canvas. What type of truck it was, I don't know, whether it was a military or a civilian vehicle because it was dark. The truck was filled quickly, they would say, "Ten of you," then, "Twenty of you." Then this one down there would call to the one upstairs. And when we climbed into the truck, it was packed full. The order was that we should sit down. We couldn't sit down when it was packed. Again, they cursed us, our balija mothers. They said, "Haris Siladzic and Alija would receive you dead and wounded." They were probably implying some sort of exchange. And again, a burst of fire at our feet and then this relative, Kadrija Becirovic, said to me, "I've been hit." And I only know that he dropped down amongst us. I know nothing more about him. And then the truck started. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you before we go on to the next part of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could show the witness five exhibits; 21/1, 21/3, 21/4, 21/5 and 21/7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a series of pictures that you've seen before in my office. Let me ask you this, Witness P, did you return to the location of that school with investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you identified that school as being the location where you were detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some pictures, a series of pictures starting with 21/1. I'm going to ask you if you can identify the buildings that are in that particular exhibit. Can you identify the buildings in that exhibit? First of all, do you see a large parking lot on the left side of the image? Now, your pointer is on a building. Can you identify that particular building? If not we'll go to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's go to Prosecutor's Exhibit 21/3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't find my way, somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. We'll go to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go to 21/3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, does this clarify the location for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the playground. Yes. The school, the entrance to the school. And this is the route we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, there is a flat area where the witness now has his pointer which is the playground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is where the trucks were [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The building in front of a playground is the school where he was detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we now turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 21/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The steps that I mentioned going down the five or six that lead to the entrance to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The double door that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness pointed to the double doors to the right side of the building. Thank you. Could we turn to 21/5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this picture, Witness P?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The steps, as I said, the landing and then the -- go upstairs and the iron rails. This is where we were; one, two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to the last picture in Prosecutor's Exhibit 21/7 and ask you if you can identify this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the vinyl tiles that I mentioned that are glued on, and to the left, a blackboard. This is the classroom, the entrance [indicates], and in the door, the chimney stack for a stove with a hole in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the location where you were detained prior to being taken out and put back on the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was here somewhere near the blackboard [indicates]. Later, I moved closer to the window. You can't see the window in this picture. So I was here somewhere [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the witness indicates "here", he's referring to a place directly under the blackboard. Thank you very much, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we'll continue with your testimony, Witness P. You said you and other men had boarded a truck. Can you recall approximately how many men were in your truck? You said it was packed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After all, it was night-time, nor could anyone count, so I don't know the figure. But imagine, 100 or so men at least. It was a big truck I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you continue, please, with your testimony, describing the events once the truck started on its next leg of the journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had climbed onto the truck after the shooting, and the truck's engine started. As soon as it started moving from the school, I saw immediately that it was a bumpy road, and we were swaying left and right and hitting each other because our hands were tied. We were standing up. The truck didn't travel for long, maybe 10 or 15 minutes. I don't know what time it was. I know it was after midnight. And then suddenly the truck stopped somewhere. At first glance, I could just see that there was a little light, that there was some sort of light reaching us. And so as soon as we stopped there, we heard heavy bursts of fire, noise, yells. I just heard someone say, "Come down ten. Come on five." And we had to run off the truck. How I got off, I don't know myself. Whether there was any assistance, some way to get off, but we were jumping off and we were all terrified. And when we got there and it was lighted, I saw a very big field of men lying dead who had previously been killed. They were all facing -- their faces were on the ground and they were all tied up. So I and this group of mine were told to form a new row, somebody was giving us the command, the orders. And so we went to the area where we were shot at with our hands tied and barefooted. I saw that the path was rocky. I was barefooted, I didn't really know where we were. I didn't know the location. So we formed a new row. We went to the end. And as we were passing at great speed, of course, I saw a group to my right of Serb soldiers in uniform, they were. And on their heads, they had something black, whether it was socks or something so you couldn't see their faces. They were pointing their guns at us and I just heard one say, "Fall to the ground." That was the order. After that, I really don't know what happened. Behind my backs, I just heard strong bursts of fire. They were shooting at our backs, at our heads. From a distance of seven to ten metres, there was this group of soldiers shooting. I fell over bodies of those who had been executed before me. As I fell, I had some kind of a premonition that I might be saved. I tried to tuck my head between the legs of those who had been killed before me. I don't know, myself, how I managed to do that. I could hear fragments and shrapnel and stones hitting me at my arms and legs, but I realised I hadn't been wounded yet. But then suddenly, something hot seemed to have been poured on my face. And as my hands were tied behind my back, I couldn't do anything. I kept digging my head down among the dead. How long this lasted, I can't remember. The shooting, the bursts of fire, I was probably unconscious again. And suddenly, I heard some voices, individual shots being fired and they were calling each other by name. One said, "Simo and Dragan, come here." And open brief bursts of fire into their heads. There must have been some men alive and indeed there were. And so they opened fire at them. He came close to me. I heard them searching the rows. And then, again, they cursed balija mothers and one said, "You should see what he looks like. He's like a skeleton." He was probably implying the chest of this man. And he said, "If I had seen him in broad daylight I would have been afraid of him." And I heard these Serb soldiers exchanging these words amongst themselves. I was lying down among the dead with my hands tied behind my back. I heard the steps. He kicked me here with his boot, with his leg and he said, "He's dead." After that, what happened with me, these were moments after which I suddenly came to. I really didn't know what had happened. I felt I was suffocating. I was lying with my face down, with my hands behind my back. And as those men were falling, someone had fallen on my neck. And I didn't have any air to breathe. I tried to pull myself out, pull my head out from among the bodies. I could hear moans and movements, so someone was still alive. And somehow -- as I said, my hands were tied. I couldn't pull free with my fingers. I heard a voice, a man saying the following words, he was whispering, "My friends, let's move down. They'll kill us. I am alive too." I plucked up some courage, and I said to him, "If you can, come on, let's try and escape." And then he somehow managed to get some five or six metres behind me in another row. He tried to reach me. He said, "You have double ropes around your hands and I can't untie you." I was whispering to him, "Can I untie you?" So he crawled up to me and I managed to pull his hands free. And he said, "Let's run." You could hear a machine approaching. We could see the lights of the machine and the sound of this vehicle moving and he said, "They'll kill us all here." And I was still tied up, he helped me get up and barefooted, covered in blood, stripped to the waist. I still didn't know where he had been wounded. We are treading over those dead bodies. And down there we saw a kind of thicket, some woods, and we thought we could reach it though the grass was high and they would be able to see us moving. But we had no choice. And only did we manage the reach the wood when we caught sight of a big concrete ditch that was leading somewhere. We didn't know the area. At the bottom of the ditch we saw a bit of water. This was water with a muddy sediment. We tried to reach that water to freshen up and for him to try and untie me. And as we were going towards this ditch to our right, or rather to our left, a vehicle was approaching. We didn't know what kind of vehicle. I just concluded that it was a tractor with a trailer. We heard it bumping over the macadam and as we reached the ditch, I said to this person, take two stones. And he found two rocks to try and cut the rope. So I leaned my hands against the rock and with those two rocks, he cut through the ropes. When he did that, my hands were freed. I saw that I had been scratched on the head. I was bloody. This other person was wounded more seriously than me. I had this vest on me. I took it off and bandaged his wound. We found a bit of water so we washed up a little. And we decided we would stay there until dawn came. This must have been just before dawn, the moments before night and day. And behind us, on the field where we had been shot at, we could hear strong fire again, noise and the noise made by the machine. We heard the thuds as they were unloading. We couldn't see from the ditch what was actually happening. As soon as daylight came, we decided to leave the area, though we didn't know where we were. We passed through a small wood. We found some mushrooms, some leaves, something to eat. And we saw a guard house, a small hut above us. And in that hut, a machine was parked. It was a bulldozer, a large bulldozer, that pushes the material in front of it with a shovel and there was a man with a rifle near that hut. Whether he had a uniform, I don't know, but he was probably a guard working for that company left over from before. So we didn't dare go ahead in that direction, so we retraced our steps, went back to the same ditch where we had been in the morning. We continued to hear explosions, the work of the machine, but we didn't know what was happening, so we were back in the ditch, and to the left of that ditch we saw a Bosniak village that had been burned down. We saw the walls still remaining, the chimneys that had been toppled and we decided we would go to that village to try and find some fruit and water to freshen up. We were barefooted and wounded. So after we had crossed the ditch, we came up on a macadam road which was passing along the Dam. So we crossed that macadam road. I was the first one to cross it, and then I motioned to him to cross it as well, because there were no vehicles. And this is where we refreshed ourselves a little bit. We found some water and we found some fruit. We must have been some 150 or 200 meters from the area where they were loading machines. So we stood there watching. We didn't dare move. We were simply lying in some brambles. We didn't know what to do. The loader arrived that morning, the one with a bucket, and it was loading dead bodies onto a tractor. I know that it was a tractor. It was a large type of tractor with very big wheels on the back and smaller wheels on the front, and it had a trailer as well. So we could see it scoop up between 10 and 15 bodies with its bucket, and then it threw the bodies onto the tractor. The tractor that was transporting the bodies would leave in a direction, but we couldn't follow it for very long, because at one point it turned off. All we could observe was that it was coming back very soon. The journey would probably last about 20 minutes, and after 20 minutes it would come back. So meanwhile the loader with the bucket, with the shovel, would be waiting for the truck to come back. We could hear shots during that time. We didn't know whether they were still killing people, finishing them off, but shots could be heard, at any rate. And we could hear them yell at each other, shout at each other. And this is where we stayed throughout the day. It was the 15th of July. It was getting dark and we knew that we could no longer stay there, so we -- from where we were standing, we could see some water. We didn't know where we were. But once we were in this village, we could see a very large lake. At first I thought it was the Drina River, but later on I found out that it was an artificial lake that belonged to the aluminum factory, would discharge waters. So there was a ditch leading to the Dam where we had been. I'm not sure that they threw bodies into the lake, but I think that they threw them somewhere in the vicinity of the Dam. We couldn't see the tractor. It would turn off behind the Dam and disappear from sight. But it would come back very soon. So we spent the whole day there, waiting, and at one point we saw the TV relay at Majevica, which was in the direction of Tuzla. So I told this young man that we should leave, that we should go in that direction, and we actually started out in the direction of the industrial area of Karakaj. The area was inhabited, so we didn't dare come out. We didn't dare cross the area. We were just trying to follow the relay, the TV transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for just a moment and let me ask you just a couple of questions to clarify your testimony. When you looked back from your position away from the killing field, can you estimate how many bodies were laying on that field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't make any estimates at the time, but judging by the features of the terrain and the number of people in the school, it must have been between 1.500 and 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you also said that you observed some heavy construction-type equipment. One was a bulldozer with a scoop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with construction equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. I knew these types of construction machines. I had worked with them. There was a bulldozer with "Caterpillar" which had a kind of blade at the front. It was not moving, that machine, the bulldozer, whereas a loader that was standing next to the bodies was. And there was a third machine, a tractor which had a trailer and which transported the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify more specifically the bulldozer with the scoop, the type of vehicle that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are several types: number 8, 9, 7. I believe it was the type number 7, with Caterpillar, with tracks. As regards the loader, this type of machine, I believe it was the ULT machine. I used to work with the same type of machines. And they were produced -- they were manufactured in Kragujevac before the war. Now they're importing them. They are of various types: 160 and 200. I believe that that one was ULT 160. It was orange in colour and it had a scoop in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you also were taken to the location of the killing field with investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor and confirmed that being the location where you and others had been taken for the execution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you four exhibits and ask you if you can confirm that the images depict the location --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There's one thing that I forgot to mention. When we got out, when we reached the village, from my vantage point I could see the Dam and I could see two very high pillars with floodlights which were on during the night. They were throwing light onto the area, onto the plateau where we had been shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for that addition. I'm going to show you four exhibits, and what I'd like you to do is merely confirm whether this is the location where the executions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could start first of all, Mr. Usher, with a panorama, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 22/3, and if that could be shown to the witness first and then placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is easier for me, this one. This is the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You need to place that on the ELMO so -- now, using the pointer, could you just -- first of all, is this the location where the killings took place, Witness P?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. So this is the road [indicates] and this is where the ditch was, the Dam [indicates]. This is a kind of protection wall [indicates]. And this is the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you point to the actual location where the killings took place in this particular exhibit, which is 22/3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, an area that is below the number 100 and to the right of the area 50, and further to the right, beyond the actual rectangle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this pile of rocks in the shape of a pyramid. This is where I was that night. And later on, when we came with the investigators, I saw it again. This is the pile of rocks [indicates]. And this is the area where we were [indicates]. And it was from there that we went down into the ditch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a pile of rocks indicated -- or shown on the diagram --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- to the right of the large red rectangle --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is the wall [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I need to describe where you're pointing, so if you would just remain silent while I have an opportunity to describe the area. Then if you have additional comments, I'll permit you to make them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness pointed to a pile of rocks which is located to the right of the red rectangle, and it's evident in the upper part of the flat surface area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have anything else to inform the Judges about this particular exhibit, Witness P?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise this wall. I remember it very well. It is a kind of support wall made of rocks. It is designed to support the Dam, the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating the pile of rocks that's in the lower right-hand corner of that Prosecutor's Exhibit. Now we'll turn to the next Exhibit, Mr. Usher, which is 22/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, very quickly, is this the cement culvert that you described in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the concrete ditch. This is where we climbed down and this is where we took shelter, hid ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is the building in the upper right-hand corner of Prosecutor's Exhibit 22/4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the guardhouse which we saw, and another structure next to it. The bulldozer was here, and these are the pillars where the floodlights were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating the bulldozer was between the house and the floodlights, which are indicated with a circle on the upper right-hand corner of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now we will turn to the next exhibit very quickly, 22/6. Is this also a picture of the cement culvert through which you and your companion found shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now if we could turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 22/7. Do you recognise what's depicted in Prosecutor's Exhibit 22/7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the road, the path leading to the Dam, and this is where we had been shot at [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating the red oval on the right-hand side of the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said at some point in time, Witness P, that you left the killing field and you took shelter in an area near some buildings that were nearby.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This would have been here, in this area [indicates]. There was a village there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating to the left-hand side of the road, the perpendicular road that comes from the top of the image down toward the Dam, to the left of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm finished with those exhibits now, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Witness P, thank you very much for identifying them. Lastly, my last question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- did you and did your companion ultimately arrive on the Bosnian-held territory, Bosnian-Muslim-held territory, on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon of the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, I've concluded my examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. I think that it would be a good idea to have a short break, perhaps a 10-minute break, and later there would be a longer break, around half past 12.00. At this point we will have a only a 10-minute break. I should like to ask the Defence to try and ask very direct and precise questions for the cross-examination. A 10-minute break. --- Break taken at 11.23 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness P, you're now going to answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Petrusic who is representing the Defence here. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning Your Honours, good morning counsel. Cross-examined by Mr.Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning Witness P.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with your suggestion, Mr. President, I will try and ask my questions in a specific manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, on the 11th of July, when you went to Susnjari, did you know that the members of the VRS had confiscated personnel carriers from the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe the witness has answered. We do not need any further clarification in respect of this. So when you started out from Susnjari towards Konjevic Polje towards the territory of Tuzla, you said that at one point the Serb soldiers mixed with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers threw hand grenades which, as far as I understand, contained some poisonous gases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, briefly, what kind of consequences did those poisonous gases have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we became very thirsty and my eyes were smarting and there were tears in our eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The fact that the Serb soldiers mixed with you and that those grenades were thrown, can we therefore conclude that the Serb soldiers were at the same territory the same night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, when they threw grenades it was on the first night it was only on the following day that the Serb soldiers mixed with the Bosnian soldiers and civilians who remained in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was on the 12th of July then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was on the 13th. The ambush was on the 12th of July in the evening and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I apologise. Were there any opposing views amongst the representatives of the Muslim population as regards the situation in which you had found yourselves, whether you should surrender or continue with the break-through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I don't quite understand what you mean by "opposing views".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, were there any different views as to what should be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean amongst the Bosnian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, people were trying to reach the right decision. Some people wanted to surrender, some were in favour of continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In view of that, were there any conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most probably there were conflicts somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At Kasaba at the football field, General Mladic spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did General Mladic mention at that point that the units with dogs were at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that there were some special units there with dogs and dog handlers, and that every inch of the forest would be covered by them and nobody would be able to cross the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After that, you left for Kravica by trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers called out people from Glogova, Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, from Kamenica, I'm sorry, Osmac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Zedansko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And those people would actually come out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, if they were from those villages. But people didn't dare speak up. But those who did were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what was the reason for that, why did they call people from those specific villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe they were their neighbours, they were perhaps looking for their neighbours, people from their area. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they mention Kravica, did they look for people from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from Kravica. It wouldn't have been possible. I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While they were calling people out, while they were looking for specific people, people from specific villages, did they also mention Kravica? And my question to you is: Did they ask who had participated in the take-over in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to show the witness, very briefly again, the statement that he gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 14th, the 15th, the 16th of August of 1995. THE REGISTRAR [Interpretation] Exhibit D-18.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On page five of the statement given on the 14th of August, 1995, second passage, the second passage from the bottom, there is a portion of highlighted text. The last sentence of the passage reads as follows, "The Serbs asked who had participated in the take over of Kravica when it fell under BH control."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know how this was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You signed this statement. Did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I interrupt? D-18 is a redacted statement so the signature of this witness has been removed. We're prepared to stipulate that the witness did, in fact, sign this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your remark, Mr. Harmon. I, myself, have realised that the witness is having some difficulties as to his signature. Mr. Petrusic, could you ask your question in a different way? Could you ask him whether he signed the statement, not whether he can see the signature on the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, your signature has been redacted from the statement so we cannot see it. So my question to you is whether this is, indeed, your statement, the one that you gave to the Tribunal's investigator on the 14th, the 15th and the 16th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it is. I cannot tell you the exact date the statement was given but I think this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you arrived in the school, the school was a two-storey building, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was only the first floor filled with people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was the first floor and the ground floor. This is what I could tell judging from the voices of the people, I believe it was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many trucks arrived in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that there had been three trucks. Two that were at the football field plus my truck. I don't know if there were any trucks later on or before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let us go back to Kravica and then I will finish with my cross-examination. Was there any reason why the Bosnian Serb soldiers would be interested for that place, in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no other questions to ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness P, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, thank you very much. Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a few questions. Good morning, Witness P.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Let me just try to clarify some points you mentioned from the beginning. You spoke of the column of almost ten kilometres when you were fleeing away and before you surrendered. And you said that one-third had weapons; is that right? One-third of you in the column had weapons. Did you use these weapons, these weapons? Had they been used against the Serbs while you were fleeing? Was there exchange of fire, some kind of fighting or were you just running away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no combats until the ambush. The people who had weapons were at the front of the column and I was somewhere in the middle of the column. And I know that there had been no fighting before the ambush, but then after I had been captured, I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when you were captured, you were captured because they announced, as you said, they asked you to surrender and that you will be exchanged; is that right, that you will be safe? But in spite of that, in spite of their reassurance, some committed suicide. What promoted this reaction if they knew that they would be exchanged? Did the Serbs give them this assurance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that they simply didn't believe. They didn't dare to believe in their guarantees, that is, that they would be exchanged, because they were killing people. They didn't pay any attention to the age, regardless of whether it was an old man or a child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there was killing before that and you could not trust them. That was the feeling you had, that already there was no reason -- there was their precedents of killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when was that, with your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But your group had started. There was no killing before that. What gave them this conviction that they would not -- that they be killed, beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that there had been an ambush, and a lot of dead bodies were scattered around the forest and people simply couldn't believe that. They were afraid of ending up in their hands. Thousands of people must have remained in the forest, so they couldn't trust them anymore when it comes to the surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was the ambush. Before that, was there any media announcing or threatening, in the media anything which gave them this conviction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war people were getting killed, and there was an order, a command, that we should go through the woods. Somebody had issued an order to that effect. People didn't dare. I don't know. They just didn't trust them. They went to the woods. A lot of people got killed in the woods and a lot of people killed themselves in the woods, because they were afraid of ending up in their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were living in Srebrenica before the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And could you listen, could you hear Serb radio and Serb television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. We didn't have electricity at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, at a certain stage, and I follow the question the Defence counsel asked you, certain people were called because they belonged to certain places. You had people coming from Osmac, they were asked to come out and so on. And as you said, after that you heard screams and gunfire. At a later stage, the order came by numbers. They would say, "Bring four people now," "Bring ten people now." Also at this second stage were these ten people or four people, were they more or less coming from a certain place or they would be without discrimination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You haven't understood me, Your Honour. I said that they were taken out individually, one by one. During the night, while I was in that truck, five people were taken off my truck. I don't know where the Serbs had come from. The trucks had canvases and they stood guard around the trucks all the time. They were working in shifts. So there would always be between 10 or 15 Serb soldiers near the trucks, and they were taking people out. And during that night, five people were taken off my truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. I then, I repeat my question more precisely. When you were in classroom 1 and classroom 2, you would hear an order, somebody saying, "Send me ten." Would he say: Send me ten from this village or that village? Or he would say: Send me ten just from the whole group, without discrimination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was in classroom number 3. And after my hands had been tied up, I was transferred to classroom number 2, that is, the next-door classroom. And they were not saying anything to that effect, anything involving a village.
