I could only hear a voice coming from outside the school, or from the entrance I would hear words, "Send me ten of them" or "Send me 20 of them." This is while I was already on the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ten of them, without saying ten of which village, or anyplace; just ten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked how many people had been lying in the killing field, you said there would be between 1.500 and 2.000. Was there enough light for you at your escape to see the extent of the lying bodies, or was it too dark? I mean, on what did you base your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could make an estimate on the basis of the number of people who had been in the school. There were three classrooms on that floor, so there must have been up to 600 people there. So I believe the same number of people would have been on the ground floor. And I believe that there were other classrooms as well. As to the area itself, I was able to observe it on the next morning, when we came out of the ditch, and also when we reached the village, because we were about 150 or 200 meters away from the spot. So I could see the whole area, and the whole area, the whole location was filled with dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness P, you told us in the beginning of your testimony that the reason that the men decided to go or were given orders to go in the woods toward Tuzla rather than to Potocari was because they didn't trust the Serbs not to kill them. They thought they wouldn't get any protection from the UN. When your group surrendered to the Serbs, what changed their mind? Why did they feel they would be able to survive if they surrendered to the Serbs, when earlier they thought they wouldn't survive if they went to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very simple. The groups had been cut off from the rest of the column, and they had a large number of wounded. And the order was that the wounded should be brought down and that we should all come down to the road. All the while there was a white personnel carrier travelling along the asphalt road, coming from the direction of Konjevic Polje -- this is what I forgot to mention -- moving towards Kravica. And it passed our group and they threw out two bottles of water. And I think that half of the people surrendered and came out onto the asphalt road because they believed it was a UN personnel carrier. And I think that it actually carried Serb soldiers, because they didn't say anything to us; they simply threw out two bottles of water when they passed by us. And again they went back in the direction of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You said you had a large group of wounded that you carried down at the time of surrender. Had most of those wounded been wounded in crossfire of an ambush, or had they been wounded just by the shelling from the Serbs? I mean, had they been wounded in an actual crossfire between the armed people in the column and the Serbs, or just as they were trying to walk along and just got shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the group was exposed to a shelling and part of the group -- people from the group were wounded in the ambush that took place on that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: During the ambush there was crossfire, right, between the Muslims who were armed in the column and the Serbian soldiers. Okay. Now, you mentioned about this incident with the poisonous gas that made the throat get thirsty and the eyes sting. Are you familiar with what's known as tear gas? I mean, sometimes police use it to break up crowds in demonstrations. It brings tears to your eyes, but it doesn't have -- so far as we know, it doesn't immediately blind anybody or anything like that. Was this something like tear gas, or was it anything you were familiar with before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you, Your Honour. I don't know. I just heard someone saying at one point that poisonous gases had been thrown at us. I wasn't very familiar with it. And I tried protect myself, to protect my face, and I was looking for a shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did this happen only once? Was this just one incident of poisonous gas or did it happen other times, or did you hear other people say that it happened to them, even if you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it from a number of people who were there, who were ambushed. I don't know what happened elsewhere or later on. I'm referring to the ambush that took place on the night between the 12th and the 13th of July. The ambush was at the location called Kamenicko, called Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: You said that from the burnt-out Bosniak village you were able to see this artificial lake near the killing fields, the one where the aluminum company dumped its refuse. Could you estimate the time it would take to drive from the killing fields to that lake? What would you guess or think it would take? How long to make the drive from the killing fields to that lake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness P, just a second. I'm sorry to interrupt. Mr. Visnjic, you were about to say something, probably in relation to "Tihomir Blaskic." I myself didn't get that as a translation or interpretation. Were you going to point to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't hear it in the French interpretation, but on the transcript I can see that there is a kind of poisonous gas that is called Tihomir Blaskic, apparently. Judge Wald, maybe you will have to repeat your question so that we can hear the answer. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know what -- on my transcript, I don't see what question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid it has already disappeared from the screen. I don't know whether it has something to do with the method used by the court reporters. Maybe we should pay attention to this aspect, we should be mindful of this particular feature of the transcript. It had something to do with a question that you asked of the witness regarding tear gas which the police sometimes uses and the poisonous gas that the witness was trying to describe. Mr. Harmon, you might help us, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I saw the name "Tihomir Blaskic" and thought it was the wrong case, but it was at a point in the transcript at 20.02.12 and it was in response -- this witness gave an answer, and what I wrote down was: "I just heard at one point that poisonous gases Tihomir Blaskic ..." and it went on. So that's the point that Mr. Visnjic stood up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Shall we ask the witness -- let me ask the question to the witness again, and the question was that whether the witness had any idea whether this poisonous gas was like the tear gas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was something like that, because the rumour spread among the people that something had been thrown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. We'll take that as your answer to the question. Now, I think we're still in the middle of the last -- well, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it would be sufficient to hear the transcript. The witness didn't mention Tihomir Blaskic. He used a word in Serbo-Croatian that sounded like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's helpful to know that. But we have his answer later on to the straight question anyway. So just to answer my last question which I had asked you about, how long you would have estimated it took to drive from the killing field to the Dam, the artificial lake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could only see from the village where our men were. We could see that lake and the field where we were executed. We couldn't get close. It is behind the hill, around a bend. You have an access road to the Dam so we couldn't really see the access to that lake. In my estimate, it would take 15 or 20 minutes to get there and back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. I think the question of transcript will be resolved as usual. The court reporters have heard the answer and will make the necessary corrections so there is no point in wasting too much time. But it has been registered in the transcript that there was a problem. Witness P, I also have some questions for you. The 13th of July, the call for surrender by Serb soldiers. In that call, they mentioned Geneva Conventions [Realtime transcript read in error "general Eva"] could you remind us in what context they mentioned the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were guaranteeing the safety of our lives and an exchange. That was at least my opinion because I had a wounded relative, and when they mentioned the Geneva Conventions that nobody could be hurt, that we would all be exchanged. So my opinion was that they would guarantee our safety, our transfer to free territory either by exchange with their vehicles or with the help of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have another type of convention. The Geneva Conventions, I think all these things have to be reviewed. We are talking about the Geneva Conventions and not the "general Eva conventions". Another question, did they expressly use the words Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I personally heard them over the loud speakers saying that we would all be exchanged in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question. Nova Kasaba, the football pitch, the whole pitch was covered. My question, were the people sitting or standing or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived, everybody was sitting down. My group and those who came after me, we all sat down on the grass field of the pitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic arrived. Did he come alone or in the company of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just saw the APC coming and I saw certain soldiers who were standing right next to the APC. At that moment, I didn't see whether anyone else came out with him, I don't remember. Of course there were the soldiers next to him, but I do know that he, himself, and alone spoke to the people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you left the football pitch, you were boarded on trucks. Those trucks, were they already there when you arrived or did they come after you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them having come there before us because trucks were passing by all the time. They were driving women and children from Potocari so trucks and buses were passing by. Some were going towards Konjevic Polje, and the others were passing towards Kasaba. So I don't know whether those trucks had come there from Kasaba and were waiting for us or did they come from some other place specially. I just know that they were empty when we came off the field and started boarding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you were at the football pitch, did you see buses passing in the direction of Bratunac-Konjevic Polje with the women and other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did see trucks and buses passing from Konjevic Polje towards Kasaba. And in the opposite direction, there were empty buses going towards Konjevic Polje probably to Potocari again to fetch some more women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness P, I have no further questions. You have answered a large number of questions put to you. Is there something that you would like to say and that you didn't have an opportunity to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to thank the International Community and this Tribunal that the truth, at least about Srebrenica, should be proven and that some kind of justice is served although that is difficult to do and that everybody should be punished for this preconceived genocide in Srebrenica. Let us take into account merely the fact that each family in Srebrenica has lost two or more family members. I lost 20 family members. My brother, their wives, aunts, cousins and so on. So I wish once again to thank the International Community and, if it can, to resolve this problem of genocide and for all the perpetrators to be punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness P, for coming. You have many years before you to live. I think you have a very good reason to live, and that is through your actions and words, you should contribute to a world avoiding a catastrophe of this kind, and I say that regardless of who is responsible. Whoever committed these acts regardless of the ethnic group they may belong to is horrific for all human beings and the human race. Witness, don't move for the moment. I think that we have some exhibits to deal with. We have Defence exhibit D-18. Mr. Harmon, I think you don't have any exhibits to tender now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't have any exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to tender into evidence Exhibit D-18, but it seems to me that the -- some redactions need to be made in the Serbian version which the witness has, but the English version has already been redacted to remove all names that might reveal the identity of the witness or other protected persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I only have a couple comments about this exhibit, but I need to go into private session to do so. It will only take a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dubuisson, shall we go into private session now, please. Please be seated, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see we are in open session now. I think, Mr. Harmon, that it would be better to have the break, which we had planned before, to have it now, give the opportunity to Witness P to leave, and when the Chamber comes back, the other witness will be in the courtroom. Will he have the same protective measures as this one, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness P, good-bye. We wish you a safe journey home. We're going to have a half hour break now and we will resume work by hearing the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Witness. The registrar is going to show you a piece of paper with your name written on it. You're going to look and tell us, yes or no, if that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is indeed your name. Are you comfortable? Are you at ease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to answer questions which the Prosecutor, in this case, Mr. McCloskey, is going to put to you. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, you know I'll be asking you some questions, and please just do your best to answer them. And if you don't know an answer, that's fine, or if you can give us estimates or rough estimates about certain things, just do your best. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to take you back to July 11th, 1995. Where were you living then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Srebrenica, the village of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was living with my parents and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you decide to do on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I decided to go to Jaglic and the family to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you decide to go to Jaglic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I didn't dare to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Well, I was afraid they would kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers that took over the town of Srebrenica, you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time on July 11th did you get to Jaglic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It must have been dark already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate of how many people were assembled there at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Ten to fifteen thousand. A large crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did the crowd decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They decided to head for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you get the word that that was the decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I heard the other men talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you decide -- or when did you actually head out with the group and go towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: On the 12th, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were near the -- farther back of the column, I guess.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you spend one night in the woods, and then, when you got near the Nova Kasaba area, get captured, on the 13th, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your capture, how that happened? Can you just try to explain a little bit who you were with and who captured you and where it happened, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. I was with ten other men. We were going to cross the asphalt road. However, Serb soldiers captured us. We didn't manage to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did anybody in the group of your ten have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. One had a pistol only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened to the pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They seized it, the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get in any firefight or any exchange of fire with this group of Serb soldiers, or did they just surround you and capture you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They just surrounded us and captured us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened after that? What did the Serb soldiers do with you, your belongings, and where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They took away our bags with food in them, then they ordered us to put our hands behind our heads and to proceed towards Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did this happen on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: About seven o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: To the elementary school in Kasaba. I think that was where the troops were, a kind of barracks, and we were imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Serb troops were in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell how many Serbs were in the barracks at that point when you were put there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: A group of some 10 to 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you put?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In a small room, like a kind of prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any Dutch soldiers around these barracks anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And had the VRS soldiers provided you with any water or food yet at this time, when you were first put into the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did they give you any water? When did they first give you water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Maybe after some 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there wounded among you when you came out of the woods and were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened when you were in the barracks, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I heard the voice of a woman crying out near Jadar. The soldiers went down there and they brought over another man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers went outside the barracks somewhere where you heard these noises coming from, and brought a man back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this was a Muslim man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And eventually were you taken somewhere else that day outside of those barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time were you taken outside of the barracks, and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: At 2.00, they ordered us to put our hands behind our backs, to go in line one by one towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you and your group then marched down the road to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say the stadium, what kind of a place was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was a football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you still in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, a little bit further from Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just right outside Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know roughly how many soldiers that were guarding your group as you were walking towards the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Two to three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the same kind of uniform the soldiers that captured you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I heard him say "yes", but I didn't hear a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be placed closer to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were the soldiers that captured you different from the soldiers that were guarding you around the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They had the same uniforms, but they weren't the same ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the soldiers that took you to the football pitch? Were those the same soldiers that were guarding you at the barracks or were those different soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The soldiers that took you to the football pitch, I think you said around three that walked you down to the football pitch, had those soldiers been guarding you at the barracks or were they new guys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They were different soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many soldiers were guarding you at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: A group was in the barracks. There was some outside as well. Ten to twenty soldiers in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got to the football pitch, can you describe the scene there; how many people, who were they, what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were about 1.500 to 2.000 men who were sitting on the field in rows surrounded by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So 1.500 to 2.000 Muslim men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give me an estimate of how many Serb soldiers you saw around them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were quite a number of them. I really don't know the number. There was an APC behind our backs. The soldiers were all around surrounding the playing field. There was no more than a metre between each one of them and the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other equipment besides this APC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I saw two more APCs on the asphalt road, and a UN APC from which no one came out. It was just standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were all these soldiers that were around the Muslim men, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this football pitch, how much of the football pitch was taken up by these Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: More than half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see any Muslim men continue to arrive while you were there at the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in what direction were they arriving from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They were coming from Konjevic Polje along the asphalt road, and they brought some from the woods. There was some who were wounded too. They bandaged the wounded and put them to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who bandaged the wounded Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how many wounded Muslims did you see get bandaged by the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the arrival of the Muslim men to the soccer field, were they arriving by foot or by vehicle of some sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you remember happening while you were there at that football pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The soldiers told us that General Mladic would come. And a short while later he came escorted by two cars and he held a speech. He told us that we would all be exchanged and that they were not criminals. He said that we should have all surrendered because not a bird could pass through their lines as there were hundreds of their lines. And he said that we would go to Bratunac for lunch. And that he would organise groups to collect the wounded in the woods, and for the dead to be buried where their families want them to be buried. Then he ordered the soldiers to make a list of the names of all those captured. At that moment, a prisoner got up and the Serb soldiers approached. They kicked him and hit him with their rifle butts. And then one soldier took out his pistol and killed him. And he was thrown into the other. Mladic was present. He didn't respond in any way. A camera was shooting the prisoners and Mladic as he was delivering his speech. When the lists were made, Mladic left towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you put your name on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see others put their name on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell if you were being filmed when you had to put your name on the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you eventually left that football pitch, about what time was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was close to dark, maybe an hour before night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were you transported away from this football pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Buses came. They stopped. They ordered us to get into the buses. When the buses were full, we started towards Konjevic Polje. We passed through Konjevic Polje towards Sandici. To the left, I saw a group of men who were sitting down in a circle surrounded by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this near Sandici that you saw these men sitting in a field surrounded by Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else did you see on your journey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I saw near Kravica on the right a kind of hangar and dead people at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit 8/4. And can we first let him take a look at that far right-hand side of the picture and then if we could put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Witness, if you could pick up the pointer and point out on the picture itself that sits on that funny machine next to you where you saw the bodies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the record should indicate that the witness has pointed to the centre of the large opening in the centre of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you were driving by, were you able to tell how many bodies were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Four or five bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you look all the way in the warehouse, or were these just the ones that were near the opening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Those were bodies that were close to the opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you notice any damage to the building that the bodies were in as you drove by it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. The traces of bullets could be seen on the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear anything going on around Kravica while you were driving by it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I heard shooting behind the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. And shortly after driving by Kravica, did you arrive to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you stop in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you spend the night on the bus in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what was written on the side of the bus that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: "Boksit Trans-Milici" was written on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of bus was it? Big bus, small bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: A big, double bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how full of Muslim men was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was very crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On your trip from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac, were there any Serb soldiers on that bus with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got to Bratunac and stopped, could you tell where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I knew that that is -- they said that we were going to Bratunac. I saw the town, so I assumed it was Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where you stopped, what kind of buildings were around you where you stopped and spent the night on that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think there was a school nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there other vehicles that also stopped in Bratunac around the same location you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were smaller cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any buses or trucks full of Muslim men at the location where you were besides your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were more buses behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell how many might have been there that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Four or five buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you tell if they were filled with Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I couldn't see, but I think that Muslims were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened that night that you stayed in this bus in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We heard shooting throughout the night, and they would take people out of the bus who never came back to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people, if you know, were taken out of your bus that didn't come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was Serb soldiers that took them out of the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think they were, because we didn't dare look. Our heads were bowed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did a Serb soldier stay on your bus all night guarding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No. They were outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many Serb soldiers were you able to see outside your bus and around that area that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but a lot of them were passing by the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: More than 20, less than 20?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Fifteen to twenty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the next morning, what happened? That would be the morning of July 14th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. The driver got out. He had started the engine and he had turned on the heating and then got out. We remained in the bus. And then it was in the afternoon and people were fainting because of the heat. Later on a soldier arrived and told us that we were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long were you in that bus with the heat going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they give you any water while the heat was going on that bus on that day? Sorry, you have to answer a little bit out loud. I know this is not easy, but the microphone didn't pick up your answer. Were you given water while the heat was going on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So finally when this soldier showed up and says you're going to be exchanged, shortly after that did the bus -- did your bus start to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It started to leave, perhaps not right away, but maybe half an hour later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did your bus drive northward up towards and through Zvornik and up to the area of Pilica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. First it was driving along a macadam road which at one point became asphalt road. We were not allowed to watch, but I noticed that it was going towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where, when you got to the Pilica area, where did the bus stop, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The bus stopped above the school, and the soldiers ordered us out and told us to run up towards the school, and they put us in a hall which was completely crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How many soldiers were on your bus trip from Bratunac to Pilica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: You mean on the buses, in the buses, how many soldiers there were?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. How many soldiers were in your bus when it drove from Bratunac to the Pilica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were those soldiers you recognised from your time in Bratunac, or were these two new people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think they were different, two new people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the school, how many soldiers did you see outside the school and around the bus that you got off of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were 15 to 20 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In camouflage uniform. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this place they took you, can you describe what kind of a hall it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was a kind of gymnasium that belonged to the school. It had baskets for basketball.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you first arrived in this gymnasium, how many Muslim men were in the gymnasium before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Less than half. Later on the hall filled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell how many buses were -- or trucks were travelling along with you on your trip to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think four to five buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you tell if there were any Muslim men in any other part of the school besides the gymnasium where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed some people on the steps. There was a very wide stairway leading to the upper floor. Some were standing and some were sitting, and we passed by on our way to the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. After you were put in the gymnasium that first day at the Pilica school and it filled up with people, did you volunteer to go get water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I volunteered together with four other men. We took some buckets and we went down the wide stairway which was on the other side past the football field. And further down, there was a tower and a water point with two fountains. When we got there, it was already dark and we started filling up the buckets with water. At that point, we heard a bus approaching the school building. Later on, we heard some noise and shooting and the guard ordered us back to the gymnasium as quickly as possible so we went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of noise did you hear before you heard the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I could hear people crying for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you tell what area around the school these cries of help were coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell what direction or what area these cries of help were coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, from behind the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'd heard a vehicle arrive before hearing the cries of help; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. I think I could hear a bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the sounds of that bus and the cries of help from the people coming from the same general area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit 23/1. Could we use one that doesn't have markings on it. I've got my copy of 23/1. I hope that doesn't confuse things too much but, I'm sorry, I didn't realise that had all those markings. And should we give it another number for the record? THE REGISTRAR [Interpretation] Yes, it will be Exhibit 24/5.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well we'll take care of that after the witness, I think, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you take a look at this photograph which has been placed on the ELMO. And first of all, could you point with your pointer the area where the bus pulled up that you were in the day you arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The bus stopped here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Indicating for the record the asphalt road or the -- well, the road right in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you enter the school? Can you point us out the entrance that you went in with that pointer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. This way [indicates] and then here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness went around to the left of the school building and then into a side entrance near the building that is perpendicular to what looks like the main building in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that building that you've got your pointer on the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the gym, that's where you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you now show us the route you took to get the -- to go down and get the water where you heard these screams and the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I got out here [indicates]. There are some steps here. We went across the football pitch, past the tower and reached this area here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, the witness went out the back of what appears to be the back of the gym by what looks like a big concrete playground, past the playground, in front of the tower and down into some trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it down by the water that you heard the bus arrive and the people call for help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And shortly after that is when you heard shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did that shooting go on for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Not for very long. Five to ten minutes because we were taken back immediately to the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you still hear the shooting when you were in the gymnasium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know about what time of day it was when this shooting started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was the night of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what occurred in the gymnasium that night, the night of the 14th, when you and all the men were crowded inside that gymnasium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. It was stuffy. Two or three men died there from lack of air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think that they were taken out by our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was anyone given any medical treatment in that gym that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the water that was brought back by you and your group enough to provide everyone with enough water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did these soldiers provide anyone in that gym with any food that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. I went out. I went to the toilet, and I know that when I got in, I fainted. And when I recovered, when I came to, I was in the corridor. A soldier gave me some pate and a piece of bread and took me back to the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see anybody besides yourself get any food that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you spend all the next day inside the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was July 15th. What happened in the gym, if anything, on that day, on July 15th, with all the people crowded in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They were taking men out. I'm sorry, I made a mistake. Could I start again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: On that day, Serb soldiers arrived and they took jewellery, watches, money from those who had them. Then they came later on again. They were asking for German marks, and they told us if we don't manage to collect the money, that we would all be killed. They came two more times, but nobody had that money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're done with the exhibit. Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentioned the amount of money, but we couldn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, I'm informed that you need to speak up a little bit more, and could you tell us the amount of money again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: 10.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did anything come of any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No. No, because nobody had that money. Whatever people had had already been taken away by the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened after they tried to take all the people's money and their valuables?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: After that, the next night, the men were being taken out from the gym. Some would come back, some didn't. The next day, I noticed that there were fewer of us in the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that night, you're talking about the night of July 15th and the morning of July 16th, you noticed there weren't as many people in the gym; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When men were taken out of the gym, did you hear any sounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there any soldiers inside the gym guarding you during your stay there or did they stay outside the gym itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, they were at the entrance to the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell how many Serb soldiers were outside the entrance of the gym and were around the school area during your stay at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were two to three soldiers at the entrance. There was a group of them in the corridor, perhaps five to ten people. There may have been 20 of them in total over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you spent two nights at this school, the 14th and the 15th. Do you know if the Serb soldiers changed shifts, or was it the same group the whole time you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think that they changed shifts, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On the morning of July 16th, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Serb soldiers came, and one of them said that some people thought that they had killed a number of young men, and he said, "Let all the young men leave the gym, one by one, because they will be exchanged." I was next to the entrance, so I stood up and got out of the gym. And as we were leaving the school building, they told us to line up against a wall, put our hands against our backs, and this is where our hands were tied up. Three buses were parked there, and we climbed onto the second bus. There were three of us sitting in one row of seats. And once the buses were filled up, they left. They started along the same road we had taken when we came to the school. At one point we turned right and reached a meadow. On that meadow I saw a large number of dead bodies. The buses stopped on a road near the meadow, and I could see a hangar there and people lying about, killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us, continue to tell us this story of what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: When the buses stopped, soldiers started taking out groups of people who were tied up. They were taking them in one column. They had to put their hands behind their backs. Those were groups of ten people which were taken to the area where the dead bodies were, on the meadow, and this is where they were killed. And then they would shoot at each one of them individually, and this is what I could observe from the bus. After the first bus had emptied, it was our turn. They took out two groups of people from my bus, and I was in the third group of people. As we were getting out of the bus, they asked if anyone had any relatives abroad so that they could send the money for the exchange, and some people spoke up and they were then singled out. And I was taken to the meadow where the bodies were. They ordered us to stop, and we stopped. There was a group of Serb soldiers there. They were in a line and they were shooting at us from their automatic rifles and from machine-guns. When they opened fire, I threw myself on the ground. My hands were still tied behind my back and I fell on my stomach, face down. And one man fell on my head. I think that he was killed on the spot. And I could feel the hot blood pouring over me. The shooting continued and then they ordered soldiers to shoot people individually. And I could hear a voice saying that they shouldn't shoot people in their heads, so that their brains wouldn't spill out, but rather to shoot them in their backs. They shot me at my back. My hands were tied on my back, but a bullet passed under my left armpit, through my shirt, and it only scratched me. And I remained there, lying. I could hear them ask if anybody was wounded. They said that they would be bandaged. And some people spoke up and then they were finished off. I could hear one man crying for help. He was begging them to kill him. And they simply said that "Let him suffer. We'll kill him later." They kept bringing in groups of people on that day, also in the afternoon, maybe for about four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 24/5. Excuse me. It's now 24/5/1. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the transcript I will correct what was said a moment ago. The previous exhibit was 23/1/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you move that over a little bit so that black dot -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, last night in my office you had a chance to look at this photograph, and could you first take the pointer and point to where your bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, he's pointing at the road that has vehicles on it that goes sort of in a -- well, it would be a north/south position, perpendicular to the road that goes across left and right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you show us the direction that Muslim men were marched to the killing fields?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, the witness has just shown us that they walked across a big open field, over to the area of a black spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did you have a chance to write in that black spot, or I helped you write in that black spot last night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I knew where it was. This is where the execution took place. And there is more over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that black spot roughly where you were when they tried to execute you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many soldiers did you see taking part in the execution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're done with that exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Ten soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many were taking part in the escorting of the victims over to the killing fields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Three or four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said you saw a machine-gun and automatic weapons. You were a soldier for some time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of machine-gun was that that you saw in the hands of the executioner?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while you were lying there, did you hear a vehicle arrive and unload something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I did. That was in the evening. We heard a vehicle. It came close to me. It unloaded something and went away again. Later, during the night, I saw that they were the bodies of killed men that were brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to -- we're going to go a little quicker now. I'll ask you a few questions which you can answer yes or no, and if you feel like you need to explain them, that's okay too. But did you spend the night on the killing field there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next day you spent some time hiding under a bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to hear anything coming from the direction of the killing fields while you were hiding under that bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I heard the sounds of machines. I couldn't see it, but I could hear it. I could hear vehicles moving, nonstop, towards that place, and going back again. This went on all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And a short time later did you come across an older man, whose name you know? But don't say who it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you and he travel together for a few days and then meet another man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that second man eventually get lost from you and the older man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then did you and the older man finally decide to turn yourselves in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you decide to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We couldn't walk any further. We were exhausted. We hadn't had anything to eat since our capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after you turned yourself in, did you go to a cafe where a Serb man looked after you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. When they captured us or rather when we surrendered, a small bus, a mini bus, there were two military policemen in it. They took us in and they drove us to a shop. They got off, sat at a table to have a drink, we stayed in the bus. Then a man came up to us, gave us each a packet of cigarettes and a pint of fruit juice, a litre and he introduced himself but I've forgotten his name. He asked us whether we were hungry. We said we were. He took us to give us food to eat and he made us coffee. Then they put us back on the bus and took us back to Karakaj. In Karakaj, there was a military truck with some 20 men on it who had also been captured. I got on to the truck, I got on to the truck. They put hand cuffs on my hands. And we were driven to Batkovici, to the camp there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What day, if you recall, were you finally released and made free?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: From the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, from the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: On the 26th of the December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we need a break now. Perhaps a short break, 15 minutes. And then the Defence will ask its questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Q, you are now going to answer questions which Mr. Petrusic, the Defence attorney, will ask you, please. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You lived in Suceska from 1992 until Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that location, Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic lived there and was militarily active there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: He was one of the commanders in the military establishment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did he or somebody from his staff issue the order for the able-bodied men to take the route you took?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The rallying of the population of that age group in Susnjari, did that take place spontaneously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: What do you mean? Could you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When I say "spontaneously", I mean that there was no order issued by anyone, any individual or body belonging to the military or the political leadership of the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know. I know I heard from others that we were going to Jaglici, to Susnjari. I never saw Zulfo, I think he must have left before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the fact that units under his command in the summer and autumn of 1992 and the winter of 1993 until the area was proclaimed a protected zone had carried out combat operations against both military forces of Republika Srpska as well as the civilian population around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, you were at the soccer pitch in Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that a list was made of those of you present there at the playing ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know, did you see who took that list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think it was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After that, you remained in the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you left the field to go towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon an hour before nightfall, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And when did you pass through Kravica, was it dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Not yet. It was dusk. Night had started to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On what side of the bus were you seated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was standing in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And this warehouse, how far is it from the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Not very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I couldn't really tell you how far it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When from the school at Pilica, you went to fetch water, you heard shots or rather shooting that lasted. From that spot, could you see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What was happening in the schoolyard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I only heard screams and shooting because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. McCloskey, have you any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Wald, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have no questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Witness Q, you have finished your testimony here at the International Criminal Tribunal. We're very glad that you managed to survive those terrible events that you were able to testify to. We wish you a safe journey home and we hope that you will have a life that will give you reason to smile again. Don't move for the moment. Mr. McCloskey, I think we have several matters to deal with this question of Exhibit 24/5.1. The exhibit submitted under that number was, in fact, 23/1.1, so we need to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm, at this point, just slightly confused about all things exhibit-wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Mr. Mark Dubuisson knows everything by exhibits and is going to explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 23/1.1 is the document shown by the Prosecutor directly to the witness and it was a photograph which was not annotated by Jean Ruez. It was a photograph of the school. And finally there is an exhibit, that is the first one that needs to be corrected. The second one is 24.5.1 an aerial photograph. Again, one that was not numbered because 24/5 was annotated by the first witness. So 24/5.1 is an aerial photograph of the execution site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also know a little bit about exhibits, don't I, Mr. Dubuisson? THE REGISTRAR [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, have you any objections regarding the admission of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. So these exhibits will be admitted into evidence as explained by Mr. Dubuisson and which I also have confirmed. I think we have to make a very short break before we begin our Status Conference. So we will only have a five-minute break. As I was saying, we need a five-minute break and we will have our Status Conference in closed session. Mr. Harmon, you have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This morning I announced that we would have two witnesses and at the conclusion of the second witnesses, we would like to tender some exhibits, some additional documents. And if we could be permitted to do that before we have the Status Conference then we can conclude the presentation of our evidence in this particular trial block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it will be better to do that afterwards. I think it is more urgent to have the Status Conference than to have those documents. Perhaps during the Status Conference I can suggest a solution to deal with that matter. I think it is more urgent to have the Status Conference than to deal with those exhibits now. So we're going to have only a five-minute break. We will come back into the courtroom without a witness. Please, Witness, don't move because of your protective measures. Good-bye, witness, therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.33, to be followed by a Status Conference 24 25
